To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the local structure of fluorine-doping in perovskite-related oxides is characterized by the presence of fluorine in tetrahedral positions, and the introduction of fluorine into the lattice leads to the reduction of hydrogen bonds.
fluorine doping of perovskite-related oxides leads to the formation of a fluorite phase.

the fluorine substitution for oxide anions in Ba2In2О5 and Ba2CaNbО5.5 double-perovskites and brownmillerites reduces the unit cell size, the fraction of hydroxy groups, and the number of strong hydrogen bonds.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effect of fluorine doping on the structure and thermal properties, including proton mobility, of fluorine-containing double-perovskites Ba2CaNb1 − xFxFxO5 and brownmillerites Ba2In2 − xFxFxFxO5 (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.4).
the local structure and thermal properties (hydration and dehydration) of fluorine-doping perovskite-related oxides.
the synthesis, structure, and thermal properties of the perovskite-related fluorinated compounds Ba2CaNb0.5 − xF1.5xO5 − 2xFx and Ba2In1.5 − xFxO5.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the introduction of fluorine ions into perovskite-related structures is a very effective method to control their structure, thermal stability and proton conductivity.
fluorine doping in the double-perovskites and brownmillerites leads to a reduction in unit cell volume due to a decrease in the average Nb–O/In–O distances.
fluorine doping in both double-perovkite and brownmilleite phases reduces the number of hydroxyls involved in strong hydrogen bonding and, therefore, the number of protonic carriers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the local structure and thermal properties in the fluorine-substituted perovskite-related solid oxides Ba2CaNb5.5 − xF xO5.5 and Ba2In5.5 −xF xO5 can be explained in the framework of a simple model based on the concept of the local structure of the perovskite and fluorite structures, which are the building blocks for these materials.
the local structure of the fluoride-doped perovскites is strongly affected by the presence of fluorine ions.
the local structure and thermal properties are affected by the fluorine substitution in both phases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
fluorine is a promising dopant for perovskite-related materials, and the fluorination of these materials is a promising way to reduce the amount of hydroxyls.
the introduction of fluorine ions leads to the formation of new hydrogen bonds, which are stronger than those in undoped compositions.
fluorine can be used for the synthesis of new perovskite-related oxides and for the modification of their physical and chemical properties.
